# Reply to Friedman {#sec-friedman}

Jane Friedman's comments are framed as a request for more detail about when, and how, interests undermine knowledge. That's a fair request, and I'm going to try to oblige. Her two complications get a section each. As it happens, the tools for answering both were sharpened in replying to McGrath, and I'll lean on the distinctions drawn there; that the same distinctions answer both sets of comments is, I hope, some evidence that they're tracking something real.

## How Interests Matter {#sec-friedman-interests}

Friedman observes that the (⋆)-based story that pins down "interests matter" in the practical cases does no work in the theoretical cases, where the mere fact of inquiring seems to do the damage. And she suggests, in a footnote, that it isn't really the inquirer's *interest* in the question but her *starting an inquiry* into it that matters. I agree with nearly all of this, and the agreement is less costly than it might look.

What matters, fundamentally, is what the proper starting points are for the inquiries a person is conducting. The inequality (⋆) is one constraint on proper starting points, possibly one among many. It is the most important constraint when the inquiry is into what maximises expected utility—a particularly important kind of inquiry, and the kind at issue in the practical cases. It is not an important constraint, perhaps not a constraint at all, in inquiries with a different shape, like the bootstrapping inquiries. So the practical and theoretical cases are indeed different at the level Friedman identifies: different inquiries, different constraints. What unifies them sits one level up: in both, a known proposition turns out not to be a proper starting point for the inquiry in progress, and that is what the loss of knowledge consists in.

Where do interests come in? The taking for granted principle quantifies over the questions one is inquiring into *or should be inquiring into*, and the two disjuncts correspond to the two ways interests matter. Interest in the everyday sense of curiosity or attention fixes which questions one is inquiring into; nobody inquires into a question they take no interest in. Interests in the welfare sense fix which questions one should be inquiring into; what makes Hiram's case different from Lois's is that, given what he stands to lose, whether the bank will really be open on Saturday is a question he *should* be asking. Two inputs, one downstream role: together they fix which inquiries' starting-point standards a person is accountable to. So Friedman is right that the view is as much inquiry-relative as interest-relative. I just don't think that's much of a shift, since the interest-facts are what determine the inquiry-facts.[^interest-pun]

[^interest-pun]: There is something suspicious in how easily 'interest' covers both roles, and I suspect it is an accident of Latin. The languages in which the same word does both jobs—*intérêt*, *Interesse*, *interés*—all borrowed it from *interesse*; languages outside that orbit tend to use different words for what is in one's interests and what one is interested in. Nothing in the theory trades on the shared word. A language that split the vocabulary would need two words to state the inputs, and one sentence to state the theory.

## Finding Out and Checking {#sec-friedman-checking}

Friedman's second complication is the sharp one. The chapter 5 cases are structurally like the encroachment cases—in both, the subject may not reason from some proposition—yet in chapter 5 the verdict is that knowledge remains and merely can't be used, while in the canonical cases the verdict is that knowledge is gone. Why, she asks, does Florian keep his knowledge while the bootstrapping inquirer loses hers? Why couldn't we say about Anisa exactly what I say about the surgeon?

Here is the shape of my answer, using the distinction between checking and finding out from @sec-mcgrath-checking. Consider two principles.

FINDING OUT
: When a person is trying to find something out—what to choose, when something happened, how likely something is—they can use any relevant knowledge.

CHECKING
: When a person is checking something—whether they locked the door, whether an instrument is reliable—they can use any relevant knowledge.

I hold that FINDING OUT is true, and exceptionless; that was the principle doing the work in @sec-mcgrath-probability. And I hold that CHECKING is false. Not wholesale: someone checking whether they locked the door can freely use their knowledge that it's a deadbolt, and which door they left by. What they cannot use is the proposition being checked, or anything whose credentials rest on it. And the explanation of that restriction is instrumental, not epistemic. Following @Melchior2019, sensitivity is necessary for checking though not for knowing: a method only counts as a way of checking whether $p$ if it would indicate that $\neg p$ in the nearby worlds where $\neg p$. A resource is admissible in a check just in case using it leaves the overall method sensitive—just in case the check would still come out differently in the nearby worlds where things are not as believed. Premising the checked proposition trivially fails that test, and so do its trivial consequences; a genuinely independent route to the same conclusion passes it, which is why re-deriving a result by a different method is a perfectly good way of checking a calculation.

This pair of principles gives Friedman the criterion she asked for. The surgeon and Florian are checking. Their minds are closed on the target proposition; the bar on using it comes from the goal of the activity; their knowledge survives, unusable but intact. The bootstrapping inquirer and red-blue Anisa are finding out. Their questions are genuinely open—that is what makes their activities inquiries—so FINDING OUT applies: they may use anything they know. Since they plainly may not use the target proposition, it follows that they don't then know it. The asymmetry between retained and lost knowledge is exactly the asymmetry between an instrumental bar and an epistemic one.

I concede that the line can be hard to see from the inside. Compare two things I might do with a big, well-regarded history book: try to find out what percentage of its claims are true, and check that it is basically reliable. These can feel the same in the moment, and my view says they differ—in the first I temporarily lose knowledge of the claims I learned from the book, in the second I keep it. But notice that the *usability* facts coincide: in both, the book-derived claims are off-limits, and usability is what shows up in deliberation. The difference surfaces elsewhere. Mid-check, "I know it's mostly right; I'm just confirming" is a perfectly good thing to say, and I can answer an unrelated quiz question with a fact from the book without embarrassment. Mid-finding-out, both look worse. So the view predicts sameness where things feel the same, and difference where a difference can be detected. It does mean that what a person knows co-varies with attitudes that aren't luminous to her. But non-luminous knowledge is not a new commitment of this book; it is close to being its thesis.
